item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Keeping the Metal Bright', 'Keeping the Metal Dark' and 'The Elegant Compromise'
item.question: You are handed a brushed-steel flask and told it should read as a light mid-grey, sitting on a background that reads near-white, in one frame. Using only what this book gives you, how do you get both?
item.answer: Treat the two surfaces as reading different parts of the same source. The flask, being close to a pure direct reflector, responds only to whatever lies inside its family of angles; the background responds to the whole source through diffuse reflection. So one large soft source can serve both: the portion of it covering the family sets the flask's tone, and the whole of it sets the background's. Having more of the source inside the family makes the metal brighter; a source large enough that little of it falls inside makes the background brighter instead. Then use distance as the second control, since the background follows the inverse square law and the metal's direct reflection does not — moving the light closer lifts the background toward white while the flask holds its tone exactly. The book's phrase for this is the elegant compromise, and the claim worth taking from it is that the metal's tone is placeable at any step between black and white independently of the rest of the scene. The bound to watch is the lens: from a close viewpoint the family is wide and the source may only just fill it, in which case the light cannot be moved without the flask's edges going black.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'The Elegant Compromise' for the single-soft-box arrangement, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light' for both the distance control and the lens bound. The matched spatula frames show the tonal independence directly.
confounders: using two lights and balancing their power, which works but misses that one large source already gives the control
expecting the metal to brighten when the light comes closer
ignoring the lens constraint, which is what makes the control fail from a close viewpoint

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.question: What does this book mean by "invisible light", and what makes the light invisible?
item.answer: Invisible light is the authors' name for lighting a subject by bouncing light off a glossy surface that sits inside the subject's family of angles while its own family of angles excludes the camera. Their worked case is a metal box on glossy black acrylic: the family of angles for the box's front face falls on the acrylic, so the acrylic is the only possible source for that face, and although the acrylic is too black to reflect diffusely it is glossy enough to reflect directly. A light placed under the camera bounces off the acrylic into the metal, which reflects it onward to the camera. The light is invisible because the camera lies outside the acrylic's own family of angles, so it cannot see the acrylic doing the lighting. The source for the box is in the scene and cannot be seen to be one.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'A Glossy Background', where the term is introduced and the geometry stated. The result is shown in the accompanying photograph of the box on black acrylic.
confounders: thinking the light is hidden behind something; it is fully in the frame and simply outside the camera's view of the reflecting surface
confusing it with the transparent-glass support, where light passes through rather than bouncing off
assuming a black surface cannot light anything, which is the intuition the source sets up in order to break

item.rationale: SPEC-01 lets an entity declare `allowed_variation: {lighting: true, viewing_angle: true}` alongside the invariants that constitute its identity. This source supplies a physical basis for setting those two flags per surface rather than per product. A matte surface's recorded brightness is independent of viewing angle, so its appearance is close to an identity property. A polished one's is not: what a mirror-like product shows is an image of its surroundings, so the same physical object legitimately looks different from a different angle or in a different room, and its centre will show whatever is in front of it. source_terms: One of the first, and most important, decisions that we have to make when we photograph a piece of metal is how bright we want it to be.
This is a critical step because it leads to two exactly opposite lighting set-ups.
the camera position is essential in any lighting diagram involving metal
item.claim: Before lighting metal, decide how bright it should appear. If bright, fill the family of angles that produces direct reflection; if dark, put the light anywhere else. Either way the first physical step is the same — find the family — but the two answers lead to exactly opposite arrangements, so the decision cannot be deferred. Because the family depends on where the camera is, a lighting diagram for metal is meaningless without the camera in it: the camera-to-subject relationship is at least as important as the subject.

mechanism.text: Polished metal is visible to the camera only through direct reflection, and direct reflection is available only from inside the family of angles, which is defined jointly by the camera position and the subject; so the light's position relative to that family fully determines the metal's tone.

scope.conditions: flat polished metal, extended by the source to metal of any shape

source_terms: because polished metal produces almost no diffuse reflection, light coming from any other angle will have practically no effect on the metal, regardless of how bright it is or how long the exposure
item.claim: Light arriving from outside the family of angles has practically no effect on polished metal, no matter how bright the light is or how long the exposure. This makes the family a hard boundary rather than a matter of degree, and it is the reason the two metal set-ups are cleanly separable: the metal's tone can be set entirely by what occupies the family, while everything outside it acts only on the rest of the scene.

mechanism.text: Diffuse reflection is the channel through which off-axis light would reach the camera, and polished metal has almost none of it; the direct channel is available only from inside the family. So off-family light has no route to the sensor via the metal.

item.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
item.question: What is Freeman doing with the abalone shell behind the quartz crystal, and what is the general permission he draws from it?
item.answer: He is using defocus to strip an object of its identity and keep only its hue. The crystal is colourless but refracts, so he placed a polished abalone shell several inches behind it and shot at a fairly wide aperture — just enough to keep most of the crystal sharp. At that distance and blur the shell is made completely abstract and unrecognisable for what it was, present only as iridescent blue and green which the crystal's facets then refract. The general permission he states is that there are times when colour will enliven an image and times when it matters less what those colours actually represent in real life.

If the metal is exposed identically in the two scenes, the background will be brighter in arrangement A and darker in B, despite the fact that the actual incident light is identical in both scenes!
if the subject is bright metal, we recommend using a longer lens and getting the camera farther away to allow more freedom in lighting
item.claim: Two cameras framing a metal subject identically — one far away with a long lens, one close with a short one — do not have the same lighting latitude. The distant camera's family of angles is narrow, so a soft box is much larger than the family and can be moved a long way without changing the metal; the close camera's family is wide, the same soft box only just fills it, and moving the light back would blacken the edges of the metal. With the metal exposed identically in both, the background is brighter in the distant arrangement and darker in the close one even though the incident light is identical. The source therefore recommends, wherever the camera position is free and the subject is bright metal, using a longer lens from farther away to maximise lighting freedom.

mechanism.text: The lens does not change the light, but the viewpoint it permits changes the width of the family of angles, and the ratio of the source's size to the family's width is what determines how far the source can be moved before it stops filling the family.

scope.conditions: bright metal where the camera position is not otherwise constrained

caveats.text: the source says this is often surprising even to highly experienced photographers, which marks it as the counter-intuitive result of the chapter
the recommendation is bounded by the coupling noted in chapter 5 — viewpoint also sets perspective distortion, and sometimes there is not much choice about where to put the camera

source_terms: the closer the metal comes to producing pure direct reflection, the closer that reflection comes to photographing at the same brightness as the light source
Black magic is anything added to the basic lighting set-up solely to place a black 'reflection' in the metal surface.
metal with dulling spray on it no longer looks brightly polished and may not even look like metal!
item.claim: A specific failure mode arises from the very purity that makes metal predictable: the closer the metal is to a pure direct reflector, the closer its reflection is to the brightness of the source, and since the surface it sits on is often the source, the two record at identical brightness and the camera cannot see where one ends and the other begins. Three finishing tools address it. Polarizing filters normally do nothing to metal, which reflects un-polarized — but the source may carry polarized rays, frequently when the metal is reflecting blue sky, and in the studio the light reflected from the surface the metal rests on is often partly polarized; where there is none, it can be introduced with a polarizer over the light. Black magic is anything added solely to place a black reflection in the surface: a gobo between a diffusion sheet and the subject gives a hard black edge, the same gobo behind the sheet gives a graduated one, softer the farther back it goes, and a soft-edged stripe of black spray paint achieves the graduation on an opaque reflector, where a gobo cannot. Dulling spray increases diffuse and decreases direct reflection, buying freedom from the family of angles at the price that the metal may stop looking like metal.

mechanism.text: An edge is visible only as a tonal boundary; when subject and background are lit to the same brightness there is no boundary to record. A black object placed inside the family of angles appears in the metal as a dark region, restoring the boundary.

scope.conditions: polished metal in a finished set-up; the source presents these as options after the basic lighting is decided

caveats.text: the source says heavy-handed dulling spray reveals rather than conceals an inability to light metal, and immediately admits all three authors keep it in their studios — an unusually candid practitioner concession

the blue-sky case explains why polarizers sometimes work on bright metal outdoors even though metal does not polarize; this is the live chapter-3 explanation (sk_lsm_c003_0019) reused, not re-extracted

item.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
item.source_locator: Ch. "Wide angle / short focal length", sub-headings "It's all about the context" and "Composition is the key" (spines 48-49)
item.question: A wide-angle landscape comes back looking empty, with the point of interest reduced to nothing. What does Carroll say happened, and what two devices does he prescribe?
item.answer: Shorter focal lengths seemingly elongate distance, so points of interest that looked relatively close to the naked eye become insignificant details lost within a wider composition. Wide-angle lenses create a lot of space in an image, so — his phrase — you really have to nail your composition. The two devices he names are leading lines and foreground interest, used to emphasise the focal points and pull the composition together. He also gives a second instruction for the near field: get close to your subject, and watch the periphery, because with a short focal length the edge detail plays an all-important role.

item.claim: The source refuses to publish lighting ratios, on the grounds that the right amount of tonal variation depends on the subject and on taste. It nevertheless states the governing distinction. A simple cube with no important detail on any side can take the full range — black shadow, white highlight. A package that has to sell a product, with important detail on all three visible sides, cannot: the highlight must be only slightly brighter and the shadow only slightly darker than the third side, because detail in either extreme would be lost. The depth clue is thereby deliberately weakened in exchange for legibility.

mechanism.text: Depth is read from tonal difference between faces, and detail is read within a face. A wide difference between faces pushes some faces into the compressed extremes of the tonal range where their detail is lost, so a subject carrying detail everywhere must accept less difference.

item.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
item.question: In the Kerala fisherman picture, what was the fast shutter speed actually spent on, and what does Freeman say happens to the frame without it?
item.answer: Not on the man. He says the straining movements of the fisherman's body were not the issue and that a modest shutter speed would have dealt with them. The 1/500 second was spent on the spurt of sand at his feet, which catches the eye because it is sharp and slightly unexpected, and which Freeman says makes the shot. His caption states the effect directly: the spurt, simply by being crisp and airborne, draws the eye down to the man's feet — and without it the immediate focus of attention is the torso. So a small frozen detail relocates the attention of the whole frame. He is measured about the size of the gain: at a slower speed the image would still have worked to an extent, but without that extra finesse.
item.support: FREEZING, converted-PDF page 142, with the attention captions on converted-PDF pages 142 and 143. The without-spurt version is a manipulation by the author, not a second exposure.

treating this as a sports-photography lesson about freezing the decisive element, when his decisive element is a by-product of the action

item.rationale: Supplies a physical account of when a surface's appearance is trustworthy evidence about the surface. Diffuse reflection is angle-independent, so a matte subject looks the same from anywhere; direct and polarized reflection are angle-determined, so a glossy subject's appearance is a fact about the geometry, not about the object. An evaluator judging whether a rendered product looks correct needs that distinction, because a shiny product photographed from a different angle legitimately looks different without any error having occurred.

applicability.when: evaluating whether a rendered or photographed subject's surface appearance is faithful
applicability.limits: The source describes physical optics with a real camera. Whether a generative model reproduces these behaviours is a Capability Lab question and is not asserted here.

item.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
item.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the opening passages on photographs as the standard of the beautiful (spine 8), and "The Image-World", the passage on how reality has come to seem (spine 10)
item.question: Sontag describes a reversal between the image and what it depicts. State it, give her example about the self, and give the boundary she puts on the claim.
item.answer: The reversal is that the copy becomes the measure: photographs, rather than the world, have become the standard of the beautiful, and instead of just recording reality photographs have become the norm for the way things appear to us — so it is reality which is scrutinised and evaluated for its fidelity to photographs. Her example about the self is exact: we learn to see ourselves photographically, so that to regard oneself as attractive is precisely to judge that one would look good in a photograph. She also reports the reversal in ordinary speech — people describing a violent event they were caught up in as having seemed like a movie, said not to diminish it but because other descriptions seem insufficient: it is how they explain how real it was. The boundary is hers and it matters: she says that in some non-industrialised countries people still felt apprehensive at being photographed, sensing a trespass, whereas people in industrialised countries seek to have their photographs taken and feel they are made real by them. The claim is scoped to the second case.
item.support: The Heroism of Vision: photographs, rather than the world, have become the standard of the beautiful; we learn to see ourselves photographically; instead of just recording reality, photographs have become the norm for the way things appear to us; it is reality which is scrutinized and evaluated for its fidelity to photographs. The Image-World: reality has come to seem more and more like what we are shown by cameras; "it seemed like a movie" is said in order to explain how real it was.

item.claim: Sontag describes a reversal in which the copy becomes the measure of the original. So successful has the camera been at beautifying the world that photographs, rather than the world, have become the standard of the beautiful — and the reversal reaches the self: we learn to see ourselves photographically, so that to regard oneself as attractive is precisely to judge that one would look good in a photograph. Generalised, the claim is that instead of just recording reality photographs have become the norm for the way things appear to us, changing the very idea of reality and of realism, so that it is reality which is scrutinised and evaluated for its fidelity to photographs. She reports the same movement in ordinary speech: people describe a violent event they were caught up in by saying it seemed like a movie, and she notes that this is said not to diminish the event but because other descriptions seem insufficient — it is how they explain how real it was.

item.definition_in_origin_frame: Put the product itself at the centre of the advertising, shown with simplicity.

item.rationale: The executable content of all seven techniques: where the camera goes, where the actors go, in what order, and how the two are timed against each other. Production IR does not exist, so none of it is translated. It is recorded in the source's frame — dollies, marks, blocking, pace — and left unbound. The geometry lives in the overhead diagrams rather than in the prose, which is noted here because a text-only reading of these objects would carry the intent without the positions.

applicability.when: a production process for creative work is eventually specified
applicability.limits: Physical staging with actors and a camera operator. No generative equivalent is asserted for any of it.

item.what_is_visible: Every image greyscale; no claim in the chapter refers to colour.
item.why_it_matters: Unlike the Albers hazard, there is nothing here for a greyscale reproduction to destroy. The films discussed are in colour, but the discussion is about sound, structure, character and lens geometry.
